extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for newspaper reporters on gathering, verifying, organizing, and writing news stories (interviewing, handling speeches/lectures, arranging copy, and composing leads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to Detect Falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons who talk for publication speak with a purpose. Sometimes their purpose is not what they say; they frequently do not tell the exact truth, even when they think they are speaking truthfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter must take into consideration the subject's mental caliber and every possible motive for acting or speaking as they do. Expect bias, excitement, grudges, or self-exploitation; use these judgments to avoid publishing false or misleading accounts (example: relatives denying a shooting, neighbors venting old grudges). Detecting falsehood readily can avoid libel suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning Everyone
rubrics_metrics.description: Because everyone sees an event from his own angle, a reporter should question everybody in any way connected with a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview Mr. and Mrs. involved, other witnesses, acquaintances in the neighborhood, servants, janitors, maids, chauffeurs, and even humble persons or children. Often servants or children will divulge facts others conceal; children may be less unstrung and more willing to tell the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Person's Previous Record
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire about the past history or previous record of the person involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past facts (divorcee, ex-convict, prior arraignments, previous sensational incidents, previously lost insured property, secret marriages, inflammatory past statements) help identify characters and may supply material for conjecture; sometimes correlation of present and past becomes the main story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Record all details while questioning different persons attempting to get all the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's easier to discard unneeded material than to return for neglected information. Learn name and address of every person connected with the story, telephone numbers, and obtain pictures of persons concerned (photos can be returned). Even apparently incidental persons may prove important later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting Names Correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Get initials, street addresses, and the spelling of names correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many libel suits start from wrong initials or addresses; misspelled names offend subjects. Verify spellings (e.g., Smith vs Smythe, Catherine vs Katharyne) and be precise—sensitivity to names matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering Speeches / Release Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an effort to get advance copies of what the speaker intends to say and a photograph of him if important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance copies (marked 'Release' with a date/time) allow accurate quoting and may let a reporter write at leisure or stay away if permitted. Respect release dates scrupulously. For nationally important speakers consult the city editor about travel to get interviews or scoops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attending Lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: When no advance copy is available, attend the lecture and secure comfortable writing arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain free tickets in advance; sit at a table near the platform. If you have a manuscript, listen for variations and indiscreet deviations. If no manuscript, take the speech by topics with occasional verbatim passages of particularly pithy lines. Do not attempt too much literal transcription—significance and spirit trump mere literalness; if verbatim is required, the city editor will send a stenographer.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Newspaper Man's Honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain news with honor—report honestly and lawfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resort to illegal or dishonest methods (stealing through windows, listening at keyholes, bribery). Fabricating or willfully distorting facts is grounds for dismissal; reputation and professional honor require honest methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of Material Before Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize news material before beginning to write to achieve speed, accuracy, and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the way back to the office use time profitably to arrange facts into a definite plan for the story so you can produce copy quickly for the city editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed is, next to accuracy, a newspaper man's most valuable asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and reorganize notes mentally or on paper to save time when typing. Having a definite plan reduces the time needed to compose and increases chance of making front page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (from Reorganization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reorganization of notes preparatory to writing aids accuracy of statement and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reporter has limited mental power; arranging and understanding notes first preserves attention for composing vivid, accurate sentences. Writing from jumbled notes risks inserting irrelevant facts or omitting important illegible items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest / Selecting an Angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story must possess a specific point or raison d'etre determined by the selection of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an angle (crime's heinousness, widow's loneliness, etc.) guided by the paper's policy and readers' interests. Selection and arrangement of details produce effects (humor, pathos); organize material with a definite motive to avoid prosaic narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Orders of Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Material may be organized by time order, space order, climactic order, or complex order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most news stories use time order or combinations; know the definitions and choose the organizational form that fits the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time Order
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple chronological arrangement of the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the norm for about 95% of news stories and can be combined with other orders; use time order for straightforward event recitals (illustrated by a child burning toes example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Space Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive writing that arranges material by physical layout or space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for descriptive pieces (example: listing victims' property after a disaster). This order explains itself through description and visual arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climactic Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange incidents so the reader does not know the outcome until the last sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective for short-story-like pieces but difficult to develop—avoid for beginners. Though rare in news copy, it is growing in popularity; use only when you can properly build suspense and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed from the known to the unknown; exposition or increasing complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when moving from familiar facts to novel or technical matters (illustrated by an AP story about an aerial torpedo boat). Often suits explanatory pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place Important Details First
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the most important details first and the least important last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers want the gist immediately. Early placement lets busy readers decide whether to continue and ensures that, if the story is cut for space, the essential facts remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for Unimportant Details (Cutability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write so the latter portions of a story can be cut without destroying the gist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early editions will be pared as the day brings more news; structure stories so the editor can prune from the end and still leave a coherent account (example: a story that can be cut at any paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of Presentation / Judicial Impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Present facts with judicial impartiality; do not willfully keep back information or distort news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arranging material avoid warping the narrative by unfair arrangement or suppression of facts. Legitimate ordering to produce an effect is acceptable, but desire for effect must not distort facts—unbiased stories are the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions from the City Editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing the reporter should brief the city editor succinctly and ask for instructions about handling the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The city editor may suggest features or tone; often he takes cues from the reporter. Competitive or unpredictable editors may prompt a reporter to prepare two or three leads to cover possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Kinds of Leads: Summarizing and Informal
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead (first sentence/group) is the more important part of the story and is of two kinds: the summarizing lead and the informal lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summarizing lead gives the gist in concise, interesting language; the informal lead introduces the reader without intimating the outcome but suggests something interesting is coming. Mastery of leads is critical to handling the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarizing Lead Details
rubrics_metrics.description: A summarizing lead may be a single sentence or several paragraphs depending on complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, brief stories usually have short leads; long, involved stories may have multi-paragraph leads (sometimes set in black-face type) that summarize parts before different divisions with their own leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: An informal lead introduces the reader to the story without intimating anything of the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to create curiosity or mood rather than to state the gist outright; it prepares the reader for an engaging narrative where the outcome is revealed later.
